title: Average Elevation Gain Per Kilometer
description: Turn a route's total climbing and distance into average gain per kilometre with Average Elevation Gain Per Kilometer — plus the grade it implies. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 850 metres of climbing over 42 km is 20.2 metres per kilometre (a 2.02% average grade) — rolling country — while a mountain trail at 1,240 m over 18.5 km hits 67.0 per kilometre and feels entirely different.
quick_answer: Average Elevation Gain Per Kilometer divides a route's total elevation gain by its distance, giving the climbing density in metres per kilometre plus the equivalent average grade. Enter gain and distance from any ride, run or hike file and read the single number that predicts how the route will feel.

Organisers quote gain; riders plan by density. The number translates a course profile into expected suffering per hour.
Weekly climbing density is a steadier load metric than weekly gain when ride lengths vary — track it and overtraining peeks out earlier.
Naismith-style estimates price climbing per distance; gain per km is the input that decides whether the 'three-hour walk' is five.
900 m over 100 km = 9.0 m/km (a big flat day). 900 m over 25 km = 36.0 m/km (a climbing day). The gain is identical; the legs will file separate reports.

body.t: Gain ÷ distance × 100: 20.2 m/km = 2.02%, 67.0 m/km = 6.70%. Average grade flattens the descents bookkeeping into one slope — useful, and precisely why it must be called average.

faq: What exactly is divided by what?
Total accumulated elevation gain (sum of all climbs in the route) divided by total route distance. Descents do not subtract — gain is climbing only, which is what legs pay for.
Where do I get the gain figure?
From your activity file: the GPX Elevation Gain Calculator computes it, and most platforms report their own version — see the threshold caveat in the comparison notes on this site.
Why do platforms disagree on gain?
Gain depends on the smoothing threshold: count every 1 m wiggle and gain inflates; threshold at 3–5 m and it shrinks. Same ride, honest different totals — compare densities only within one method.
Start-to-finish difference is a different (much smaller) number — a loop's net is zero while its gain may be 900 m. This calculator uses accumulated gain, the effort number.
Feet per mile is offered alongside metres per kilometre (20.2 m/km ≈ 106 ft/mile) — same density, local dress.
The metric prices climbing only. Technical descents cost time the number cannot see — one reason mountain-bike densities and road densities are not comparable across sports.
